title: Train, validation, test
story:
Three jobs get confused because they all involve running a model against data that is not the training data. Fitting parameters, choosing between options, and estimating what you will get in production are separate activities, and each one contaminates the next if it is allowed to use the same rows.

The first split is the one everyone knows. Parameters are fitted on the training portion, and the general rule, stated bluntly in the documentation, is never to call the fitting method on the test data — which also covers the cases people miss, since the same applies to every preprocessing step, and the risk is relevant with almost all transformations rather than being a peculiarity of a few.

The second split is the one that gets skipped, and the reason it exists is subtle enough to be worth spelling out. Suppose you have a training set and a test set, and you try forty model configurations, checking each against the test set and keeping the best. Nothing you did was cheating in any obvious sense — you never fitted on the test data. But the number you report is the maximum of forty noisy measurements, and the maximum of forty draws is systematically higher than any single draw. You have selected on noise, and the winning score is optimistic by roughly the amount of noise present. Do it enough times and you have fitted the test set by hand, one decision at a time.

That is the formal point made by Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold and Roth: approaches to ensuring validity of inferences assume a fixed procedure selected before the data are examined, while in practice data analysis is intrinsically adaptive, with new analyses generated based on data exploration and on the results of previous analyses on the same data. Every choice made after looking at a score is an adaptive step, and the guarantees were never stated for those.

So the third portion exists to be spent. The validation set is the one you are allowed to consult repeatedly — it is there to be selected against, and its score is understood to be optimistic. The test set is looked at once, at the end, after every decision has been made, and its score is the estimate you report. If you look at the test set and then change something, you no longer have a test set; you have a second validation set, and you should say so.

The awkward part is that nothing enforces any of this. There is no error and no warning. The discipline is procedural, and the only real safeguard is writing down in advance how many times the final portion may be consulted, and treating that as a budget rather than an aspiration.

problem.name: Three-way data partition
problem.shape: The same data is being asked to fit parameters, choose among models, and estimate future performance, and those three uses interfere with one another.
tell: many configurations were tried and the best score is being reported
there is a training set and a test set and nothing between them
a decision was made after seeing the final score
nobody can say how many times the held-out data has been consulted
problem.move: Give each job its own portion. Fit on the first, select on the second as often as you need, and consult the third once, after every decision is made. Decide in advance how many times the third may be looked at, and if you consult it and then change something, relabel it as a validation set and obtain a new one.
problem.invariant: A score used to choose among options is a property of the selection, not an unbiased estimate of performance. The maximum over many noisy measurements exceeds the truth by roughly the noise, whether or not any fitting touched those rows.
problem.breaks: Nothing in any tool enforces the separation, because no rule is technically violated when you look. The contamination accumulates one decision at a time and leaves no trace in the code, so the only evidence is a record of how the decisions were made — which is not part of the artefact.

cost.space: data withheld from training twice over, which is the real price and is felt most on small datasets
cost.beats: a two-way split with repeated consultation, which produces a number that reads like an estimate and behaves like a selection

worked.problem: Why three sets rather than two?
worked.reasoning:
Because choosing and measuring are different jobs, and a score cannot do both without becoming optimistic.

The two-way split handles fitting. Parameters are estimated on one portion and evaluated on another, so the evaluation is not a measure of memorisation. That part is well understood.

What it does not handle is selection. Suppose you try forty configurations and pick the one scoring best on the held-out portion. You never fitted on those rows, so nothing obviously wrong happened — but the reported number is the maximum of forty noisy measurements. Each configuration's score is the truth plus some noise, and taking the maximum picks up whichever one got the luckiest noise as well as whichever is genuinely best. The winner's score is therefore biased upward by roughly the scale of the noise, and the more options you try the worse the bias gets. You have fitted the held-out set by hand, one decision at a time, with no fitting method called anywhere.

This is why the discipline is about procedure rather than about code. The formal version is that validity arguments assume a procedure fixed before the data are examined, while real analysis is intrinsically adaptive — new analyses are generated from exploration and from the results of previous analyses on the same data. Every decision made after seeing a score is one of those adaptive steps.

So the third portion has a specific role. The validation set exists to be spent: consult it as often as the work requires, select against it freely, and understand that its final score is optimistic. The test set is consulted once, after every decision is settled, and its score is what gets reported. The two are not interchangeable and the difference is not the data — it is how many times each has been looked at.

The rule I would state for the awkward case, because it comes up constantly: if you look at the test set and then change anything, you no longer have a test set. You have a second validation set. The honest response is to say so and, if a clean estimate genuinely matters, to obtain data that has not been consulted.

And where data is too scarce to split three ways, the answer is nested cross-validation rather than reusing one held-out portion for both jobs — an inner loop that selects and an outer loop that estimates, which preserves the separation at the cost of computation.

problem.practice: Take a model you have tuned and count honestly how many configurations were compared against your held-out data. Then hold out a fresh portion that has never been consulted, score the chosen model on it, and compare the two numbers. The gap is what the selection cost you.

beats.broke: The same data cannot both choose a model and measure it, because once a number has been used to select among options it is a property of the selection rather than an estimate of anything.
beats.fix: Give the three jobs three portions — one to fit the parameters, one to choose between models, and one looked at once, at the end, to estimate performance.
beats.cost: Three portions means less data for each, and the discipline is procedural rather than technical: nothing in the code stops you consulting the last one, and every consultation spends a little of what it was reserved for.

interview.q: Why three sets rather than two?
interview.trap: Answering that the third is a safety margin or a second opinion. The reason is specific: the best of many noisy scores is biased upward by roughly the noise, so a set used for selection has already been fitted by hand even though no fitting method was ever called on it.
interview.answer:
Because choosing and measuring are different jobs, and one score cannot do both without becoming optimistic.

A two-way split handles fitting: parameters are estimated on one portion and evaluated on another, so the evaluation is not measuring memorisation. What it does not handle is selection. Try forty configurations and keep the one scoring best on the held-out portion, and you never fitted on those rows — but the number reported is the maximum of forty noisy measurements. The formal version is that validity arguments assume a procedure fixed before the data are examined, while real analysis is intrinsically adaptive, with new analyses generated from exploration and from earlier results on the same data. Every decision taken after seeing a score is one of those adaptive steps.

So the roles differ. The validation set exists to be spent: consult it freely, select against it, and accept that its score is optimistic. The test set is consulted once, after every decision is settled, and its score is what you report. The difference between them is not the data, it is how many times each has been looked at.
